clue.text: State provided mountain peaks

parts.note: Mass is the standard abbreviation for Massachusetts, a US state
provided means if, as in 'provided it rains'

explanation.surface: A remark about a region granted some mountain summits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' is not a verb meaning say: it is a US state, Massachusetts, shortened to MASS.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains, a mass of high ground with several summits.

clue.text: Lunatic hasn't. the head to be a.:publicist.

indicators.note: lacking its head means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a lunatic is a madman

explanation.surface: A madman who has lost his mind ends up working in advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hasn't the head' drops the first letter of MADMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An adman writes advertisements, so he publicises products.

clue.text: Play defensively, in general

explanation.surface: Advice to a sports team to play cautiously, in broad terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in general' looks like 'generally', but Stonewall Jackson was a Confederate general in the American Civil War. In cricket, to stonewall is to bat purely defensively.
explanation.definitionFit: To block cautiously without scoring is stalling play; Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson was a famous Confederate commander.

clue.text: Topple the reputation of an opponent

indicators.note: toppling something turns it upside down, which in a down clue reads the run backwards

parts.note: a reputation is a name, as in 'make a name for yourself'

explanation.surface: A plan to ruin a rival's good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topple' turns NAME OF upside down, giving FO EMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for an enemy, an adversary in battle.

clue.text: Co-operate, as Nausicaa was wont to with her maidens

definitions.text: as Nausicaa was wont to with her maidens

explanation.surface: A classical allusion: the princess Nausicaa and her attendants at their games.
explanation.walkthrough: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus is woken by the princess Nausicaa and her maids playing a ball game on the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means go along with others; literally it is what Nausicaa did, tossing a ball with her attendants.

clue.text: Deceitfully, what I pretend not to celebrate

indicators.note: a deceitful arrangement disguises its letters, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses, a little slyly, to the thing they pretend not to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deceitfully' rearranges all fifteen letters of WHAT I PRETEND NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means go out on a boisterous spree of partying.

clue.text: Saw greenfly devouring yellow marigold head

indicators.note: one word eating another holds it inside

parts.note: aphis is the singular of aphids, greenfly
or is the heraldic word for gold or yellow

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A garden scene: aphids eating the flower of a yellow marigold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' is not the tool or past of see, but a saying. Or is the heraldic gold; 'devouring' puts it inside APHIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, a pithy maxim.

clue.text: Dice give help to Commissioner. Sanders

explanation.surface: Throwing dice could assist a police commissioner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories, Lieutenant Tibbetts, nicknamed 'Bones', is the assistant to District Commissioner Sanders.
explanation.definitionFit: Dice were once carved from bone, hence the slang; Bones is Sanders's sidekick in the Wallace tales.

clue.text: Teach girl to become languid

indicators.note: these letters are to become something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructing a girl so that she turns listless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to become' rearranges TEACH GIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy, just like languid.

clue.text: Deliveries grabbed. by mischievous beggar

indicators.note: something grabbed by another is held inside it, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: mischievous means impish, like a playful imp
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, so deliveries are overs

explanation.surface: A naughty tramp snatching parcels that were being delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beggar' looks like a noun, a vagrant, but here it is the verb meaning reduce to poverty. Deliveries are cricket OVERS, not parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: To beggar someone is to ruin them financially, leaving them destitute.

clue.text: Fruit — bananas?

explanation.surface: Is that fruit, or are they bananas?
explanation.definitionFit: Hazels and walnuts are dry fruits; 'bananas' and the answer are both slang for crazy.

clue.text: Carbon and nitrate, 'when mixed, have an effect on each other.

definitions.text: have an effect on each other

indicators.note: chemicals mixed together are jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A chemistry lesson: carbon and a nitrate react when combined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when mixed' shuffles C and NITRATE into the answer; the chemistry surface hides that 'Carbon' is just its symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that act upon one another mutually influence each other.

clue.text: Old corps takes on a trainee, a rogue

parts.note: RASC was the Royal Army Service Corps, a British army unit since renamed
L stands for learner, as on a British learner driver's L-plate

explanation.surface: A former army unit enlists a recruit who turns out to be a scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: RASC is the Royal Army Service Corps, a former British army corps; L is the learner plate on a British trainee driver's car.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a scamp or villain, a dishonest or mischievous person.

clue.text: Second part of 'Don Juan' produces a new star

indicators.note: only the latter half of the word is kept, the first half dropped

parts.note: a Don Juan is a womaniser, like the famous Venetian lover Casanova

explanation.surface: A theatre review: the second act of the opera Don Juan creates a fresh celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second part of' keeps the back half of CASANOVA, a byword for a seducer like Don Juan, dropping CASA. The theatre surface makes 'star' look like a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly brightens, once thought to be newly born; Latin nova means new.

clue.text: At once uncontrollable

explanation.surface: A sudden description of something running wild.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means immediately, without thought; it also means out of control, like unruly children.

clue.text: Second-can interfere in 'old woman's. battle

indicators.note: to interfere in something is to get inside it, so these letters go within the other word

parts.note: a hag is an ugly old woman; the possessive gives an S
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A busybody suggests a second container could meddle in a grandmother's fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Battle of Hastings, 1066, is the famous English battle of the Norman Conquest.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1066 clash between Harold and William the Conqueror is named after this English town.

clue.text: Baffling noise bull makes

indicators.note: makes signals that the letters make up something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bewildering sound that a bull produces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' rearranges NOISE BULL.
explanation.definitionFit: An insoluble problem cannot be solved, so it is puzzling.

clue.text: Fellow in female attire caught sneering…

indicators.note: the fellow is placed inside the garment

parts.note: a sari is a garment worn by women in South Asia
a don is a fellow of a university college
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A man in women's clothing was spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: DON goes 'in' SARI, then C, the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sardonic means mocking and scornful, grimly derisive.

clue.text: Sturdy tool about in the beginning.

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the beginning is the start

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the tool's word is read backwards

parts.note: an awl is a pointed tool for piercing holes

explanation.surface: A robust implement turns up right at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns AWL into LWA, which goes 'in' START.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalwart means strong, robust and dependable, like a loyal supporter.

clue.text: Container for wine

explanation.surface: A bag holding wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A bag is a container; sack was also an old name for dry white wine such as sherry, Falstaff's favourite.

clue.text: .skirt-like garment has. .to droop round a fellow

indicators.note: the drooping word goes round the name, holding it

parts.note: to droop is to sag
Ron is a man's name, any fellow

explanation.surface: A wrap-around skirt sags around a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' wraps the drooping word around a man's name. The ellipsis carries on from 17 down's sneering man in women's clothes, so the garment fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarong is a length of cloth wrapped round the waist, worn in South-East Asia.

clue.text: Supply retired physician of note

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or drawn back, so the whole run is read backwards

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, a physician
fa is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A notable doctor who has stopped practising provides something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' reverses the whole run of three pieces. 'of note' looks like 'famous', but 'of' gives its own letters and 'note' is a sol-fa syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: To afford can mean to provide or yield, as when a window affords a view.

clue.text: In conclusion,/ring has a 'stone upside down.

parts.note: the ring-shaped letter O

indicators.note: in a down clue upside down means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a gem is a precious stone

explanation.surface: Finally, a ring has its jewel set the wrong way up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upside down' turns A GEM into MEGA.
explanation.definitionFit: The last letter of the Greek alphabet stands for the end, as in 'alpha and omega'.

clue.text: We have a' twenty shilling sovereign about, not an 18

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the monarch's word goes around the pound sign, holding it

parts.note: a sovereign is a king
twenty shillings made a pound in old British money, abbreviated L from Latin libra

explanation.surface: We own a gold coin worth a pound, but not a solid one.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 across is STALWART, so 'not an 18' means a feeble person. A sovereign was also a pound coin worth twenty shillings in old British money, which tempts you to read it as a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone weak and puny is the opposite of a sturdy stalwart.

clue.text: From just within earshot, comes closer

indicators.note: the letters come from just a part of the words, a run lying within them

explanation.surface: Someone just audible is approaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just within earshot' reads like 'barely audible'; the letters run across 'withiN EARShot'.
explanation.definitionFit: To near something is to approach it, getting closer.

clue.text: Watch out for the hole in the ground

explanation.surface: A warning about an opening in the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave!' (Latin, beware) was British schoolboy slang for 'look out, a teacher is coming'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin imperative means beware, a lookout's warning; a hollow in rock or earth is a cavern.

clue.text: Managed to turn dinghy, a vessel intended for inland waterways

definitions.text: a vessel intended for inland waterways

indicators.note: turning the word round means reading it backwards

parts.note: managed means ran, as in ran a business
a dinghy is a small rowboat

explanation.surface: Someone succeeded in turning a small boat round on a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' reverses RAN to NAR. A narrowboat is the long, slim British canal boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A long slim boat built to fit Britain's narrow canal locks.

clue.text: Lent brought forward

explanation.surface: A lent sum, moved earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Money advanced is money lent ahead of time; a date advanced is moved earlier.

clue.text: Freely agrees to provide lubricant

indicators.note: freely means loosely, without fixed order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone willingly consents to supply oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freely' looks like it describes the agreeing, but it rearranges AGREES.
explanation.definitionFit: Grease is a thick oily substance used to reduce friction in machinery.
